extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in internet culture, memes, and 4chan
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and document aspects of 4chan's role in internet culture, including meme origins, formats, collective actions, controversies, and platform-specific practices. This page is a descriptive encyclopedic account of memes, incidents, and cultural effects related to 4chan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lolcat format
rubrics_metrics.description: A lolcat is an image combining a photograph of a cat with solecistic text intended to contribute humour, widely popularized by 4chan in the form of a weekly post dedicated to them and a corresponding theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the constituent elements of the lolcat meme (photograph + intentionally misspelled/solecistic caption) and notes 4chan's role in popularizing them via recurring themed posts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bait-and-switch / rickroll meme genesis
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2005, the installment of a word filter which changed "egg" to "duck", and thus "eggroll" to "duckroll", across 4chan led to a bait-and-switch meme in which users deceitfully linked to a picture of a duck on wheels. This was then modified into users linking to the music video for Rick Astley's 1987 song "Never Gonna Give You Up". Thus, the "rickroll" was born.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates how small technical/site changes (word filters) and playful deception (bait-and-switch links) can produce enduring meme formats; shows the stepwise transformation from one prank format to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misspelling-driven meme formation ("an hero")
rubrics_metrics.description: The term "an hero" [sic] became a synonym for "suicide" after a misspelling in the Myspace online memorial of seventh grader Mitchell Henderson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of how accidental misspellings or nonstandard orthography can be recontextualized into meme language; demonstrates a pathway from real-world text to memetic shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to leetspeak
rubrics_metrics.description: 4chan and other websites, such as the satirical Encyclopedia Dramatica, have also contributed to the development of significant amounts of leetspeak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States 4chan's role in evolving online coded language (leetspeak); implies criteria for meme-language innovation include community adoption and repeated use across posts/sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes used as symbols to mock or signal (Pedobear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedobear ... is often used within the community to mock contributors showing a sexual interest in children. Pedobear is one of the most popular memes on non-English imageboards, and has gained recognition across Europe, appearing in offline publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how a meme can function as a rhetorical device or symbol within and beyond the site (mocking, signaling), and how such usage can cross into offline contexts and be repurposed (including problematic uses such as graffiti).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymous attribution norm
rubrics_metrics.description: 4chan has been labeled as the starting point of the Anonymous meme ... due to the norm of posts signed with the "Anonymous" moniker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies a cultural/behavioral norm (unified anonymous signing) that produced a collective identity (Anonymous) and facilitated organized memetic and real-world actions (e.g., Project Chanology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet raids and collective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Users of 4chan and other websites 'raided' Hal Turner by launching denial-of-service attacks and prank calling his phone-in radio show... The site's users have managed to pull off some of the highest-profile collective actions in the history of the Internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes a pattern where coordinated online community actions (raids, DoS, prank calls, hacking) are used as collective expression or disruption; examples illustrate scale and legal/financial consequences for targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform for distributing leaked or private material
rubrics_metrics.description: On August 31, 2014, a compromise of user passwords at iCloud allowed a large number of private photographs taken by celebrities to be posted online, initially on 4chan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes 4chan's role as an initial dissemination point for leaked/stolen content and the platform responses (e.g., announcing enforcement of a Digital Millennium Copyright Act policy and banning repeat posters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meme propagation and remixing (example: "Chocolate Rain")
rubrics_metrics.description: A link to the YouTube video of Tay Zonday's song "Chocolate Rain" was posted on /b/ on July 11, 2007, and then subsequently circulated by users, becoming a very popular internet meme. The portion of the song in which Zonday turns away from the microphone, with a caption stating "I move away from the mic to breathe in", became an oft-repeated meme on 4chan and inspired remixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates meme lifecycle on the boards: discovery/posting, rapid circulation, selection of a repeatable fragment, captioning, and remixing—key mechanics of memetic spread and mutation.
